name: text/turtle
description:
Turtle is how most people actually write RDF. It is the W3C's compact text syntax for a graph: prefixes declared once with `@prefix`, `a` standing in for rdf:type, and semicolons and commas so one subject can carry many statements without being named again.

The RDF 1.1 Turtle Recommendation defines it, and it sits deliberately between two neighbours. Take every abbreviation out and what remains is [application/n-triples](/application/n-triples). Add named graphs and it becomes [application/trig](/application/trig). The XML serialisation that came first is [application/rdf+xml](/application/rdf+xml).

name: application/n-triples
description:
N-Triples is the line-based subset of Turtle: one statement per line, every term written out in full, no prefixes and no abbreviations at all. The W3C Recommendation calls it easy to parse, which is the entire design goal.

Being verbose to read is what makes it convenient for everything else. A file can be split at any newline, streamed, sorted, diffed or compared line by line, which is why a format invented for test cases became the usual way to ship bulk RDF. Add graph labels and it becomes [application/n-quads](/application/n-quads); add abbreviations and it becomes [text/turtle](/text/turtle).

name: application/trig
description:
TriG is Turtle extended to write down a complete RDF dataset rather than a single graph. Statements are grouped into named graphs, each introduced by the IRI naming it, alongside a default graph for anything left unattributed.

Named graphs are what let a store record where a statement came from, or when it was asserted, without altering the statement itself. Everything [text/turtle](/text/turtle) can express, TriG expresses the same way, so Turtle is the subset to reach for when one graph is all there is. The line-based form of the same dataset is [application/n-quads](/application/n-quads).

name: application/n-quads
description:
N-Quads is N-Triples with one more element on each line, an optional graph label after the object, which turns a file of statements into a whole RDF dataset. The W3C Recommendation puts it plainly: the main distinction from [application/n-triples](/application/n-triples) is that N-Quads can encode multiple graphs.

Everything that makes N-Triples convenient survives the addition. Each line still stands alone, so a dataset of any size can be streamed, sorted or split without a parser holding state. The readable form of the same dataset, with prefixes and grouping, is [application/trig](/application/trig).

name: text/n3
description:
Notation3 came first and Turtle is the part of it that stays inside RDF. What was left behind is the interesting half: N3 adds variables and implication, so a document can state a rule and not only a fact, and a reasoner can then derive conclusions nobody wrote down.

It also treats a graph as a term, which allows statements about statements. The registration cites the 2008 W3C Team Submission, while the language is now maintained by a W3C Community Group. Anything that only records facts is better written as [text/turtle](/text/turtle), which every RDF tool can read.

furtherReading.title: W3C Notation3 (N3): A readable RDF syntax

name: text/shaclc
description:
SHACL validates RDF graphs against shapes, and SHACL's own syntax is RDF, which makes a shapes file precise and tiring to read. The compact syntax is an alternative notation for a subset of SHACL Core, aimed at people editing shapes by hand.

It is not a second language. A compact document maps to the RDF form and back, so tools keep working. The specification began in the RDF Data Shapes Working Group and continues in the SHACL Community Group, so it is not a Recommendation. The other way to describe the shape of a graph, with a grammar of its own rather than a second syntax, is [text/shex](/text/shex).

name: text/shex
description:
Shape Expressions describe what an RDF graph has to look like: which properties a node carries, how many values each may have, and what those values must be in turn. This type names the compact syntax, which reads like a grammar; the same schema also has JSON and RDF forms.

ShEx and SHACL answer the same question and are easy to mix up. ShEx was built as a schema language with a notation of its own, developed in a W3C Community Group. SHACL is written in RDF and became a Recommendation, then added [text/shaclc](/text/shaclc) to solve the readability problem ShEx never had.
